The Seat of Our Pants lets you go ahead and cry about it but makes sure you leave laughing.
The Seat of Our Pants is the Thornton Wilder adaptation we didn’t know we needed in the theatrical canon.
The Seat of Our Pants, Ethan Lipton’s musical adaptation of Thornton Wilder’s The Skin of Our Teeth, is both pleasant and entertaining.
It’s spruced up and better decorated, but the bones haven’t been touched.
But honestly, that pretty much says it all.

I witnessed the premiere of The Seat of Our Pants at The Public Theater, and found the show to be pretty much a dud both as a musical and a production, only sporadically brightened by lively performances.
The Seat of Our Pants is one of those unhappy events when a group of gifted people take on a project that simply goes bust.
Lipton, Silverman, and their extraordinary cast haven’t simply added songs to Wilder’s strange epic; they’ve added heart, humor, and a theatrical wink that makes the impossible feel joyous.
Lipton’s genius is recognizing that musicalization shouldn’t tame Wilder’s chaos—it should add another layer of theatrical self-awareness.
Fans of Wilder will rejoice at this fresh take on a genuine classic.
A fantastic cast gamely attempts to justify this musical adaptation, but The Seat of Our Pants never answers why Thornton Wilder’s masterpiece needed singing in the first place.

But watching the cast, led by wonderful performances by Grotelueschen (Into the Woods, Pericles) and Diamond (Parade, The Cher Show), having so much fun — even band member Allison Ann Kelly gets in on the action — is infectious.

cn.t: Lipton's musical adaptation of Wilder's notoriously difficult play earns mostly positive reviews for its self-aware embrace of absurdity and timely relevance, though some critics question whether musicalization solves or complicates the original's challenges.
